title: Deserializing a Schema
background:
JSON Schema documents are usually authored and stored as JSON text. In application code, that means one common workflow is to load schema text and turn it into a `JsonSchema` object before evaluation.

This approach is useful when schemas come from configuration files, embedded resources, or remote content. It also mirrors how many production systems manage validation rules outside compiled code so that constraints can evolve without rebuilding the app.

In this lesson, schema text is provided. Make it usable for validation.
instructions: Load `schemaText` as a schema and use it to validate the instance.

title: Evaluate a Schema
background:
After a schema exists, the core workflow is to evaluate an instance and inspect the resulting EvaluationResults. This is the central call used throughout the library.

In this lesson, a schema and instance are already in place; the goal is to get the validation result.
instructions: Evaluate the provided instance with the schema and return the evaluation results.

title: Direct Construction
background:
JsonSchema can be created in several ways, depending on your input source. Common options are `JsonSchema.FromText(...)` for schema strings, `JsonSchema.FromFile(...)` for file-based schemas, and `JsonSchema.Build(...)` when you already have a `JsonElement` to build from.

Choosing between these methods is mostly about where schema content comes from in your application. In this lesson, a parsed `JsonElement` representing the schema is already available. Use it to produce a working schema.
instructions: Construct a schema from the provided `schemaElement` and use it to validate the instance.

title: Schema Builder: Any String
background:
`JsonSchemaBuilder` gives you a fluent, type-safe way to compose schemas directly in C#. Each method call adds one keyword to the schema under construction.

Builder-based schema authoring is especially useful when your constraints are assembled dynamically from business rules, user configuration, or feature flags. It can also improve readability when you want schema definitions to live close to application logic.

This lesson starts with the simplest possible constraint: require that the instance is a string.
instructions: Produce a schema that accepts any string value.

title: Schema Builder: Number with Limits
background:
Numeric constraints are one of the most common validation tasks in API and domain modeling work. JSON Schema supports precise numeric boundaries, including inclusive and exclusive limits.

With `JsonSchemaBuilder`, numeric rules are easy to express with fluent calls such as `.Maximum(...)`, `.Minimum(...)`, and `.ExclusiveMinimum(...)`. Combining these keywords lets you model practical rules like ranges, thresholds, and allowed intervals.

In this lesson, produce a schema that fits those boundaries.
instructions: Produce a schema that accepts numbers greater than 0 and at most 10.

title: Schema Builder: Nesting Schemas
background:
The `JsonSchemaBuilder` class provides a type-safe fluent interface for building schemas in code. Adding a keyword is accomplished by calling the same-name (usually) extension method.

Some keywords take schemas.  To do this with _JsonSchema.Net_, you'll want to pass a nested `JsonSchemaBuilder` into the `.Items()` extension method.

To help make your code prettier, there is an implicit cast from `JsonSchemaBuilder` to `JsonSchema` that automatically calls the `.Build()` method so you don't have to.
instructions: Produce a schema that accepts an array of integers with no more than 5 items.

title: Build Options: Local Schema Registry
background:
By default, schema resolution can rely on globally registered schemas. That works, but it can create coupling across unrelated validation flows. Build options allow using an isolated registry so reference resolution is scoped to one build path and does not depend on global process state.

In this lesson, a referenced schema is already defined. Configure build-time resolution so the reference is resolved from a local registry. Another independent build-time option is dialect selection, which is covered next.
instructions: Build a schema named `schema` that references `sharedRule` using the local build configuration.

title: Build Options: Dialect Selection
background:
Dialect selection is another build-time lever alongside registry configuration. Build options are applied while constructing schemas and determine how keywords are interpreted. Setting the dialect explicitly gives predictable behavior instead of depending on defaults.

In this lesson, the schema uses a `format` keyword that must behave as a hard constraint rather than just an annotation; choose the right build configuration to make that happen. Once that baseline is set, the next step is controlling evaluation-time format enforcement.
instructions: Ensure the schema is built targeting the v1/2026 dialect.

title: Evaluation Options: Require Format Validation
background:
Now that we've reviewed how dialect can influence format behavior at schema-build time, this lesson shifts to evaluation-time control. In cases where the active dialect or runtime configuration does not require format assertions by default, format keywords may behave like annotations unless evaluation is configured to enforce them.

In this lesson, the schema includes a format constraint; make evaluation enforce it.
instructions: Make the schema enforce the `format` keyword when evaluating instances.

title: Evaluation Options: Custom Formats and Local Registry
background:
Format validation is controlled at evaluation time and can be scoped locally. Combining a custom format definition with a local format registry keeps behavior isolated to a single evaluation flow.

In this lesson, a `web-color` format is referenced in the schema but has no built-in definition; give the evaluator what it needs to validate that format.
instructions: Add support for the `web-color` format so instances are validated against it.

title: Evaluation Options: Detailed Output
background:
Evaluation output can be shaped for different goals. `OutputFormat.Flag` returns only pass or fail, which is useful for quick gates. `OutputFormat.List` returns a flat set of result nodes, which is useful for summaries and reporting. `OutputFormat.Hierarchical` preserves schema structure in the result tree, which is useful for debugging and mapping errors back to nested schema sections.

In this lesson, configure evaluation to use hierarchical output so you capture a complete, structured breakdown of failing constraints.
instructions: Configure evaluation so that all constraint failures are captured in the output details.

title: Generation: Essentials
background:
Many applications already have strongly typed domain models that describe the shape of their data. Schema generation lets you derive JSON Schema from those types so validation and model definitions stay aligned.

Using `.FromType<T>()` reduces duplicate authoring work and helps avoid drift between handwritten schemas and the C# types your code actually uses. It also makes schema generation repeatable as models evolve.

In this lesson, a simple `Person` type is provided. Use it to derive validation rules and apply them to the instance.
instructions: Derive a schema from the `Person` type and use it to validate the instance.

title: Generation: More Constraints
background:
Schema generation is already wired up in this lesson. The next step is tightening the generated rules by annotating your model with generation attributes.

Attributes such as `[Required]`, `[MinLength(...)]`, and `[ExclusiveMinimum(...)]` let you express business constraints directly on properties so generated schemas enforce more than just basic type shape. In this lesson, add the attributes needed for required names and a positive age rule.
instructions:
Add `FirstName`, `LastName`, and `Age` properties to the `Person` class, and add attributes that provide the following constraints:

- all properties are required
- `FirstName` and `LastName` must be at least two characters long
- `Age` must be greater than 0

title: Generation: Nullability
background:
After adding required and range constraints with attributes, the next step is expressing nullability rules in generated schemas.

Nullability semantics in JSON Schema are not the same as C# nullability annotations alone. Use `[Nullable(...)]` to explicitly control whether the generated schema allows `null` for a property.
instructions: Add a `DateTime` property called `BirthDate` and mark it as nullable.

title: Generation: Conditionals (Simple)
background:
Validation rules are not always universal; some should apply only in specific situations. Conditional validation lets constraints activate only when specific model values are present.

In generated schemas, attributes such as `[If(...)]` and conditional required rules let you express `if`/`then` behavior directly on the model type. In this lesson, make `Cylinders` required only when `Type` is `petrol`.
instructions: Add generation attributes so Cylinders is required only for petrol-powered propulsion models.

title: Generation: XML Comments
background:
After shaping validation behavior with constraints and conditionals, the next improvement is schema documentation. Generation can read XML `<summary>` comments from types and properties and emit them as `description` keywords.

This helps make generated schemas more understandable to downstream consumers and tools without hand-writing documentation into the schema itself.
instructions: Add some XML comments to the `Person` type to generate a `description` keyword.

title: Validated Serialization: Manual Schema
background:
A robust ingestion pipeline usually validates payloads before mapping them into application types. Validation catches structural and domain rule violations early, before invalid data reaches business logic.

With a manually authored schema, you have full control over each constraint and can tune the exact rules you want to enforce at system boundaries. This is especially helpful when models are shared across services or when contract governance is strict.

In this lesson, a JSON payload arrives as a raw string. Keep invalid data from reaching the application layer.
instructions: Validate the payload first and only deserialize it when validation succeeds.

title: Validated Serialization: Generated Schema
background:
Generated schemas are useful when your domain model already expresses most of the constraints you care about. By generating from the model type, you reduce duplicate authoring and keep validation rules aligned with the code that consumes the data.

Even with generation, the safest flow is still validate first, deserialize second. This keeps invalid payloads out of your object graph and gives you a clean point to produce helpful validation feedback. The same pattern also maps well to service boundaries, where `JsonSchema.Net.Api` can apply schema-based validation in API pipelines.

In this lesson, protect deserialization with the constraints already expressed by the `Person` model.
instructions: Validate the payload against the `Person` model's constraints and only deserialize when it passes.
